prompt: A grower claims that stressing Cannabis always increases THC. How should Grow Doc evaluate that claim using replicated field evidence from high-CBD hemp?
expected_points: A replicated field study tested several environmental and biotic stress treatments across three high-CBD hemp cultivars and found generally limited effects on cannabinoid profiles.
The study reported no evidence that the tested stresses increased THC concentration or the THC-to-CBD ratio at harvest, while herbicide treatment decreased cannabinoid content.
Grow Doc should reject the universal claim that stress always boosts THC and keep any stress-effect statement tied to the specific treatment, genotype, tissue, timing, and study conditions.
forbidden_claims: Any stress treatment can be used predictably to boost cannabinoid potency

source_metadata.title: Limited effect of environmental stress on cannabinoid profiles in high-cannabidiol hemp (Cannabis sativa L.)

prompt: What does controlled floral-hemp drought research say about cultivar variation, and what should Grow Doc avoid turning into a universal drought rule?
expected_points: Controlled greenhouse work comparing floral-hemp cultivars found that stronger water stress reduced several physiological performance measures.
The study also found cultivar-related differences in water-use efficiency and drought response, showing that genotype can affect measured performance.
Grow Doc should not convert one experiment's drought intensity, timing, or cultivar response into a universal threshold or expected outcome for every Cannabis cultivar and production system.
forbidden_claims: All Cannabis cultivars have the same water-use efficiency under drought
One greenhouse drought threshold applies to every production system

source_metadata.title: Identifying physiological traits related with drought tolerance and water-use efficiency in floral hemp (Cannabis sativa L.)

prompt: A grower says that if total nitrogen stays the same, the ammonium-to-nitrate ratio cannot materially change Cannabis yield or secondary metabolism. Using the controlled medical-Cannabis evidence, correct that claim without turning one experiment into a universal feed recipe.
expected_points: Saloner and Bernstein held total nitrogen at 200 mg/L while varying the ammonium-to-nitrate ratio, so the experiment directly tested nitrogen form rather than simply changing total nitrogen supply.

Under the tested controlled conditions, increasing the ammonium fraction generally reduced plant performance, inflorescence yield, and secondary-metabolite production; 50% ammonium produced toxicity symptoms late in maturation and 100% ammonium caused severe damage and plant death.

Grow Doc should conclude that nitrogen form can matter even when total nitrogen is held constant, while keeping any ratio recommendation conditional on the cultivar, developmental stage, nutrient system, environment, and endpoints studied.
forbidden_claims: Only total nitrogen concentration matters in Cannabis nutrition
The study proves one ammonium-to-nitrate ratio is universally optimal for all Cannabis grows

source_metadata.title: Nitrogen Source Matters: High NH4/NO3 Ratio Reduces Cannabinoids, Terpenoids, and Yield in Medical Cannabis
